      "body": "As noted in https://www.mail-archive.com/openssl-dev@openssl.org/msg46709.html, OpenSSL has code that is \"available\" rather than \"released\". That aside, TLSv1.3 is still a draft and is not yet standardised. Additionally, we are well aware of the draft implementations in BoringSSL and OpenSSL."

    {
      "id": 298235345,

      "id": 298235621,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-298235621",
      "created_at": "2017-04-30T14:32:54Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 5",
      "body": "nginx has only added support for `TLS1.3` in the `ssl_protocols` directive. https://github.com/nginx/nginx/commit/9a37eb3a62130473596e0e4c2e388d80bdb14956"

    {
      "id": 298266061,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-298266061",
      "created_at": "2017-05-01T00:05:58Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 6",
      "body": "You know, I am really thinking that those who are dying for a draft implementation of a not yet ratified standard could run code from other projects with a proven track record of draft quality implementations of not yet ratified standards.... "
    },
    {
      "id": 372156611,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-372156611",
      "created_at": "2018-03-11T22:45:53Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 7",
      "body": "TLSv1.3 is still a draft and is not yet standardised largely due to industries that make a lucrative trade on SSL/TLS intercept products for enterprises not yet knowing how to \"break\" the protocol and allow it to properly proxy across their appliances.\r\n\r\nPlease dont let draft prevent the inclusion of an important advancement of the protocol.  "
    },
    {
      "id": 375914594,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-375914594",
      "created_at": "2018-03-24T18:29:31Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 6",
      "body": "Amazing. I would not have known any of that if someone hadn't posted it\ninto a github PR..\n\nOn Sat, Mar 24, 2018 at 5:19 AM, Denis Denisov <notifications@github.com>\nwrote:\n\n> The Committee IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), engaged\n> <http://www.ietf.org/mail-archive/web/ietf-announce/current/msg17592.html>\n> in the development of protocols and architecture of the Internet, approved\n> the final version of the specification\n> <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-tls13/> defines a TLS\n> 1.3, as the \"Proposed standard\" (Proposed Standard). Those involved in the\n> development of TLS Protocol members of the working group (Transport Layer\n> Security Working Group) were able to reach consensus and voted to\n> standardize the 28 draft specifications (all voted \"Yes\", excluding Warren\n> Kumari <https://research.google.com/pubs/WarrenKumari.html> from Google,\n> who voted \"I don't mind\", explaining\n> <https://www.ietf.org/mail-archive/web/tls/current/msg25562.html> that he\n> is not an expert on the issue under discussion). The installation of secure\n> connections using TLS 1.3 is already supported in Firefox and Chrome, and\n> will be offered in the OpenSSL 1.1.1 branch.\n>\n> Features of TLS 1.3:\n>\n>    - Disposal of obsolete and unreliable cryptographic primitives (MD5,\n>    SHA-224) and capabilities (compression, re-negotiation, non-AEAD ciphers,\n>    static key exchange RSA and DH, specifying a unix-time in Hello-messages,\n>    etc.);\n>    - In mode perfect forward secrecy (PFS, Perfect Forward Secrecy\n>    <https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_forward_secrecy>), in which the\n>    compromise of one of the long-term keys does not allow you to decrypt\n>    previously captured sessions. Leaving only PFS support caused a lot of\n>    controversy <https://www.cs.uic.edu/%7Es/musings/tls13-enterprises/>\n>    and became a stumbling block in reaching consensus, as a number of\n>    manufacturers pointed to the possible negative impact of PFS on corporate\n>    systems, on-premises networks of which are used\n>    <https://www.ietf.org/mail-archive/web/tls/current/msg21275.html>\n>    inspection of passing traffic, for example, to ensure fault tolerance,\n>    monitoring, problem diagnosis, malware filtering and detection of attacks.\n>    - Reducing the number of steps in soglasovanii connections and mode\n>    support 0-RTT <https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-0-rtt/> to\n>    eliminate delays in the resumption of the previously established HTTPS\n>    connections. When you install an HTTPS connection are 4 stages: DNS lookup,\n>    TCP Handshake (1 RTT), the TLS Handshake (2 RTTS to the key agreement\n>    parameters and an encrypted channel) and send a HTTP request (1 RTT).\n>    Compared to TLS 1.2 in the new standard, the number of RTT for TLS\n>    Handshake is reduced from 2 to 1, i.e. for the installation and resumption\n>    of a connection requires a DNS query and 3 of the communication cycle (RTT)\n>    instead of 4. 0-RTT allows you to save the previously agreed parameters of\n>    the TLS and to reduce to 2 the number of RTT when resuming a previously\n>    established connection;\n>    - Support for the ChaCha20 <http://cr.yp.to/chacha.html> stream cipher\n>    and the Poly1305 <http://cr.yp.to/mac.html> message authentication\n>    algorithm developed by Daniel Bernstein (Daniel J. Bernstein\n>    <http://cr.yp.to/djb.html>), Tanja Lange (Tanja Lange), and Peter\n>    Schwabe (Peter Schwabe). ChaCha20 and Poly1305 can be considered as faster\n>    and safer analogues of AES-256 CTR and HMAC, the software implementation of\n>    which allows you to achieve a fixed run time without using special hardware\n>    accelerators;\n>    - Support for secure Ed25519 <http://ed25519.cr.yp.to/> authentication\n>    keys, which have a higher level of security than ECDSA and DSA, with a very\n>    high rate of verification and signature creation. Resistance to cracking\n>    for Ed25519 is of the order of 2^128 (the average for the attack on\n>    Ed25519'll need to make 2^140 bitwise operations), which corresponds to the\n>    resistance of different algorithms such as NIST P-256 and RSA with the key\n>    size of 375 bytes, or 128-bit block cipher. Ed25519 is also not affected by\n>    problems with the collisions in the hashes are not sensitive to attacks\n>    over the definition of the speed of the cache (cache-timing attacks\n>    <http://cr.yp.to/antiforgery/cachetiming-20050414.pdf>) and side\n>    channel attacks (side-channel attacks);\n>    - Support key exchange based algorithm x25519\n>    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve25519> (RFC 7748\n>    <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7748>) x448 and (RFC 8031\n>    <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8031>);\n>    - Support HKDF <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HKDF> (HMAC-based\n>    Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function).\n>\n> —\n> You are receiving this because you commented.\n> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub\n> <https://github.com/libressl-portable/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-375874633>,\n> or mute the thread\n> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/AHv2dQtpDBMul6JHlV_aUxYDEdI_LyEJks5thivdgaJpZM4KEGQu>\n> .\n>\n"
    },
    {
      "id": 375916733,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-375916733",
      "created_at": "2018-03-24T19:00:56Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 6",
      "body": "We will support 1.3 once the standard is firmed up and finalized (i.e. ceases to be coopted by vendors making changes to allow for people to continue to run moribund middle boxes that can't recognize a new protocol on the wire)  Since there is effectively nothing wrong with TLS 1.2 with a sanely chosen cipher suite today, we believe a clean careful implementation is more beneficial than early adoption. "
    },
    {
      "id": 375942759,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-375942759",
      "created_at": "2018-03-25T03:32:47Z",
      "updated_at": "2018-03-25T03:34:32Z",
      "author": "Participant 7",
      "body": "FWIW 1.3 was finalized and approved by the IETF last wednesday.\r\nhttps://www.ietf.org/mail-archive/web/ietf-announce/current/msg17592.html\r\ninteresting inclusion of a controversial feature, 0-RTT.\r\n\r\nplease check:\r\nE.5.  Replay Attacks on 0-RTT\r\n\r\nin my opinion this should probably remain a secure-by-default \"off\" feature unless a gas leak in the users office has convinced them to enable it for some reason.\r\n\r\nThanks again for your dedication and careful consideration.  "
    },

      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-655751976",

      "author": "Participant 9",
      "body": "Forgive me if this is not in the scope, as I'm not fully up to speed on the inner workings of TLS. But I've been having trouble with OpenVPN compiled against LibreSSL 3.1.3 connecting to a server (ProtonVPN) which uses a TLS 1.3 cipher, specifically `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`. The TLS handshake fails.\r\n\r\nProblem is, I'm not seeing it listed in:\r\n```\r\n▶ openvpn --show-tls          \r\nAvailable TLS Ciphers, listed in order of preference:\r\n\r\nFor TLS 1.3 and newer (--tls-ciphersuites):\r\n\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA384\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA\r\nDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384\r\nDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA256\r\nDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305\r\nECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305\r\nDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305\r\nGOST2012256-GOST89-GOST89\r\nDHE-RSA-CAMELLIA256-SHA256\r\nDHE-RSA-CAMELLIA256-SHA\r\nGOST2001-GOST89-GOST89\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA256\r\nECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA\r\nECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA\r\nDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256\r\nDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256\r\nDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA\r\nDHE-RSA-CAMELLIA128-SHA256\r\nDHE-RSA-CAMELLIA128-SHA\r\n```\r\n\r\nIf client side was enabled, is there a reason I don't see it listed here? Do I need to compile it myself with additional build flags?\r\n\r\nThanks for any help.\r\n\r\n___\r\n\r\nEdit: and sorry, I realize that's output from OpenVPN, but I also checked with:\r\n```\r\n▶ libressl ciphers\r\nAEAD-AES256-GCM-SHA384:AEAD-CHACHA20-POLY1305-SHA256:AEAD-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA:DHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:DHE-RSA-AES256-SHA256:DHE-RSA-AES256-SHA:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:DHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:GOST2012256-GOST89-GOST89:DHE-RSA-CAMELLIA256-SHA256:DHE-RSA-CAMELLIA256-SHA:GOST2001-GOST89-GOST89:AES256-GCM-SHA384:AES256-SHA256:AES256-SHA:CAMELLIA256-SHA256:CAMELLIA256-SHA:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA:DHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:DHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256:DHE-RSA-AES128-SHA:DHE-RSA-CAMELLIA128-SHA256:DHE-RSA-CAMELLIA128-SHA:AES128-GCM-SHA256:AES128-SHA256:AES128-SHA:CAMELLIA128-SHA256:CAMELLIA128-SHA:ECDHE-RSA-RC4-SHA:ECDHE-ECDSA-RC4-SHA:RC4-SHA:RC4-MD5:ECDHE-RSA-DES-CBC3-SHA:ECDHE-ECDSA-DES-CBC3-SHA:EDH-RSA-DES-CBC3-SHA:DES-CBC3-SHA\r\n```\r\n\r\nand don't see it there."

      "created_at": "2020-10-19T18:55:34Z",

    {
      "id": 712384413,
      "url": "https://github.com/libressl/portable/issues/228#issuecomment-712384413",
      "created_at": "2020-10-19T19:11:06Z",
      "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 10",
      "body": "On Mon, Oct 19, 2020 at 11:55:56AM -0700, leonklingele wrote:\n> Does that mean v3.2.2 should bring TLS 1.3 support to nginx? Cause It's not working for me :(\n\nThis is expected.\n\nnginx does its own version selection and turns off TLSv1.3 unless\nTLS1_3_VERSION is defined:\n\nhttps://github.com/nginx/nginx/blob/master/src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c#L364-L367\n\nWe can't define TLS1_3_VERSION publicly yet since this would break other\nsoftware that assumes OpenSSL TLSv1.3 API to be present if TLS1_3_VERSION\nis defined. We didn't have time to implement and test this API before\nthis release.\n\nPassing -DTLS1_3_VERSION=0x0304 on nginx's compiler command line\n(CFLAGS) or adding\n\n```\n#ifndef TLS1_3_VERSION\n#define TLS1_3_VERSION 0x0304\n#endif\n```\n\nbefore the lines linked above would make nginx use TLSv1.3.\n"
    },

    {

      "author": "Participant 6",
      "body": "On Mon, Oct 19, 2020 at 11:55:52AM -0700, leonklingele wrote:\n> Does that mean v3.2.2 should bring TLS 1.3 support to nginx?
